slides.title: Resolution, viewport and aspect ratio
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “The question”; glossary, 2D art and sound assets; Godot docs, Multiple resolutions (viewport).
slides.notes: The 1,024 × 873 file and the 640 × 360 viewport are from Chapter 2, “The question”. The scale factors are computed.
slides.picture: The image file, then the viewport beside it at the same scale, then their aspect ratios, then the image scaled by one factor and by two different factors.

new_texts: THE IMAGE FILE, DRAWN AT HALF SIZE
The resolution is a fact about the file: 893,952 pixels.
all_texts: THE IMAGE FILE, DRAWN AT HALF SIZE
The resolution is a fact about the file: 893,952 pixels.

new_texts: The area the game draws into, set in Project Settings; the window scales it.
The file is 1.60 times wider and 2.42 times taller than the viewport.
The viewport is the game's own size; the file is bigger, so it must be scaled down.
all_texts: The area the game draws into, set in Project Settings; the window scales it.
The file is 1.60 times wider and 2.42 times taller than the viewport.
The viewport is the game's own size; the file is bigger, so it must be scaled down.

new_texts: WIDTH ÷ HEIGHT, BOTH DRAWN 150 PX TALL
The ratios differ, so no single scale can make the image fill the viewport exactly.
Different shapes: scaling to fill would change the picture, not just its size.

new_texts: Same factor on both axes versus different factors that distort.
The circle in the file becomes an ellipse on the left.
Use one factor (the smaller, 0.412) and accept bars; two factors squash the art.

slides.title: Texels, nearest and linear, integer scaling
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “Texture settings that decide whether a sprite survives”; glossary, 2D art and sound assets.
slides.notes: The 6 × 6 sprite is invented. Shade counts and pixel widths are computed from it.
slides.picture: A 6 by 6 sprite with one texel marked. Then the same sprite enlarged to 24 by 24 with nearest and with linear filtering. Then widths of enlarged pixels at three scales.

new_texts: 6 × 6 = 36 texels; the file stores each one
A texel is a pixel counted inside the texture, before it is drawn.
all_texts: 6 × 6 = 36 texels; the file stores each one
A texel is a pixel counted inside the texture, before it is drawn.

new_texts: Nearest reads one texel and keeps hard edges; linear blends four and smooths.
THE SAME SPRITE DRAWN 4 TIMES LARGER (24 × 24)
Every blended shade is a grey that is not in the art.
Nearest keeps 2 shades. Linear invents greys. Pixel art needs nearest, set on the node.
all_texts: Nearest reads one texel and keeps hard edges; linear blends four and smooths.
THE SAME SPRITE DRAWN 4 TIMES LARGER (24 × 24)
Every blended shade is a grey that is not in the art.
Nearest keeps 2 shades. Linear invents greys. Pixel art needs nearest, set on the node.

new_texts: Scaling by whole numbers so pixel art stays crisp.
ON-SCREEN WIDTH OF EACH SPRITE PIXEL (SCREEN PIXELS)
Whole-number scales keep every pixel the same width; 2.5 makes some pixels 50% wider.
all_texts: Nearest reads one texel and keeps hard edges; linear blends four and smooths.
Scaling by whole numbers so pixel art stays crisp.

slides.title: Sprite sheets, atlases and frame rate
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “Frames: SpriteFrames and AnimatedSprite2D”; glossary, 2D art and sound assets and Animation section.
slides.notes: Cell size 48 × 48 is from the Chapter 2 exercise. The 5 FPS default is from Chapter 2.
slides.picture: A strip of four frames in cells of 48 pixels, then one frame cut out as a region, then an animation list playing at 5 frames a second, then 5 against 12 frames a second.

new_texts: One image of many frames in a grid.
ONE IMAGE FILE: 4 CELLS OF 48 × 48 PIXELS
cells are equal and the same scale, so a test can count them
A sheet is an image; the frames are fixed cells in it.
all_texts: One image of many frames in a grid.
ONE IMAGE FILE: 4 CELLS OF 48 × 48 PIXELS
cells are equal and the same scale, so a test can count them
A sheet is an image; the frames are fixed cells in it.

new_texts: Many small images packed into one big texture; a frame is a region of it.
A FRAME IS A REGION OF THE SHEET
Godot cuts a frame as an AtlasTexture: the sheet plus a rectangle.
all_texts: One image of many frames in a grid.
Many small images packed into one big texture; a frame is a region of it.

5 FPS is a new animation's default

slides.title: Alpha, transparent backgrounds, PNG and JPEG, fringe
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “Ideas you need”, items 1 and 4; Chapter 7, finding F-2 (JPEG, no alpha); glossary, 2D art and sound assets.
slides.notes: Memory sizes are width × height × channels. The halo is computed by mixing stored colours.
slides.picture: Nine pixels from alpha 0 to alpha 1 over a checkerboard. Then a baked checkerboard against a real cutout. Then PNG and JPEG channels. Then an edge with and without a halo.

new_texts: ONE PIXEL AT NINE ALPHA VALUES
alpha is the fourth channel after red, green and blue
Alpha 0 is see-through. A game sprite needs it at every background pixel.
all_texts: ONE PIXEL AT NINE ALPHA VALUES
alpha is the fourth channel after red, green and blue
Alpha 0 is see-through. A game sprite needs it at every background pixel.

new_texts: Cut the background to alpha 0; ask for a solid colour, not for transparent.
corner pixel: alpha 1. The checkerboard is painted pixels.
corner pixel: alpha 0. The level shows through.
A requested transparency can come back as a painted checkerboard. Check the corners.
all_texts: Cut the background to alpha 0; ask for a solid colour, not for transparent.
corner pixel: alpha 1. The checkerboard is painted pixels.
corner pixel: alpha 0. The level shows through.
A requested transparency can come back as a painted checkerboard. Check the corners.

new_texts: Lossless with alpha versus lossy without alpha.
the same 1,024 × 873 image, uncompressed in memory
A JPEG has no alpha, so a JPEG sprite keeps its white box. PNG keeps alpha.
all_texts: Cut the background to alpha 0; ask for a solid colour, not for transparent.

ONE EDGE, SAMPLED IN 12 STEPS, OVER A DARK RED LEVEL
left of each strip: the sprite edge; right: transparent texels
Filtering blends in the colour of transparent texels. Fill them with the edge colour.

slides.title: Import settings, lossy copies and mipmaps
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “The import pipeline” and “Texture settings”; glossary, 2D art and sound assets.
slides.notes: The three import lines are from Chapter 2. The lossy row is modelled by averaging, not by a real codec.
slides.picture: A source file, its .import text file and the cache. Then a row of pixels kept exactly or averaged. Then a chain of mipmaps from 256 down.

new_texts: Per-asset options controlling how the engine converts it, kept in the .import file.
commit the .import file; do not commit .godot/
Godot never uses your PNG or WAV directly. A text file beside it records the conversion.
all_texts: Per-asset options controlling how the engine converts it, kept in the .import file.
commit the .import file; do not commit .godot/
Godot never uses your PNG or WAV directly. A text file beside it records the conversion.

new_texts: Exact reconstruction versus smaller files with lost detail.
Single-pixel details are the first thing a lossy copy loses.
For pixel art, Lossless is recommended. Lossy trades small files for lost detail.
all_texts: Per-asset options controlling how the engine converts it, kept in the .import file.
Exact reconstruction versus smaller files with lost detail.

new_texts: Pre-shrunk copies of a texture used when drawn small; about 33% more memory.
A 256 × 256 TEXTURE AND ITS SHRUNK COPIES
= 133.3% of the original: about 33% more memory
Drawn at 1/4 size, the engine reads the 64 × 64 copy.
Mipmaps help when art is drawn small. A 2D sprite at 1:1 does not need them.

slides.picture: A coloured bug beside the same bug filled black. Then the bug at 436, 96 and 48 pixels, and the 48 pixel version magnified with its legs faint.

new_texts: The outline of an object; it should still read when filled black at game size.
FILL IT BLACK: DOES THE SHAPE STILL SAY WHAT IT IS?
The black-fill test removes colour and detail. What is left is what the player sees first.

436 PX → 96 PX → 48 PX (DRAWN AT HALF SIZE)
a 4 px leg becomes 4 ÷ 9.08 = 0.44 px wide
under one pixel: drawn at 44% strength, a faint smear
Readable at 1:1 in the real scene beside the player, not in an image viewer.

slides.title: The collider is not the art
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “The collider is not the art”; glossary, Game movement and collision.
slides.notes: 18 × 28 is the player collider in Chapter 2. The 42 × 34 art size is invented.
slides.picture: A character drawn larger than its 18 by 28 collider. Then the art flipping while the collider stays. Then a spike that overlaps the art before it hits the collider.

new_texts: Shape used for contact tests; separate from the art and sized from the body.
the art reaches 12 px past each side of the box
The box is sized from what the player believes is solid: the body.
all_texts: Shape used for contact tests; separate from the art and sized from the body.
the art reaches 12 px past each side of the box
The box is sized from what the player believes is solid: the body.

new_texts: FLIP THE ART: THE COLLIDER STAYS
keep the collider a sibling of the sprite, not its child
Mirroring the art would mirror the collider too, if it were a child. Keep it a sibling.
all_texts: Shape used for contact tests; separate from the art and sized from the body.
FLIP THE ART: THE COLLIDER STAYS
keep the collider a sibling of the sprite, not its child
Mirroring the art would mirror the collider too, if it were a child. Keep it a sibling.

new_texts: THE SPIKE OVERLAPS THE ART, THEN HITS THE BOX
the spike overlaps the art for 12 px before a hit
fair if thin or decorative; unfair if it looks like the part that hurts
Art past the box is a design choice. Write down why.

slides.title: PCM, sample rate, Nyquist limit and synthesis
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “Procedural audio is not generative audio”; glossary, 2D art and sound assets.
slides.notes: 440 Hz at 22,050 Hz is the generator demo in Chapter 2. All numbers are computed.
slides.picture: Stems for one cycle of a 440 hertz tone sampled at 22,050 a second. Then the same tone at 22,050 and 2,000 a second. Then a chart of the pitch heard against the pitch played. Then the first six values of the formula.

new_texts: ONE CYCLE OF A 440 HZ TONE AT 22,050 SAMPLES A SECOND
each stem is one number between −1 and 1
the list of numbers is the PCM data
PCM is the plain list: one number per sample.
all_texts: ONE CYCLE OF A 440 HZ TONE AT 22,050 SAMPLES A SECOND
each stem is one number between −1 and 1
the list of numbers is the PCM data
PCM is the plain list: one number per sample.

new_texts: SAME TONE, TWO SAMPLE RATES, ONE CYCLE EACH
2,000 a second: 4.5 samples per cycle (a crude copy)
More samples per cycle give a closer copy; 2,000 a second gives about 4.
all_texts: SAME TONE, TWO SAMPLE RATES, ONE CYCLE EACH
2,000 a second: 4.5 samples per cycle (a crude copy)
More samples per cycle give a closer copy; 2,000 a second gives about 4.

new_texts: The highest frequency a sample rate can hold: half the rate.
PITCH HEARD VS PLAYED AT 22,050 A SECOND
a 15,000 Hz tone is heard as 7,050 Hz
Above half the rate, a pitch folds back down: 15,000 Hz sounds like 7,050 Hz.

a formula, not a recording and not a generative model

slides.title: WAV and Ogg, loop point, one-shot
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2, “Sound: import, loop, trigger”; Chapter 12, “Import”; glossary, 2D art and sound assets.
slides.notes: The waveform is invented. 4.000 s, 44,100 Hz and loop end 176,399 are from Chapter 2.
slides.picture: A 4 second waveform with sample numbers. Then loop begin and end markers with a moving playhead. Then a looping lane beside a one-shot lane. Then a loop cut in the middle of a cycle against one cut at zero.

new_texts: WAV for short effects; Ogg Vorbis for music, speech and long sounds.
4 S MUSIC LOOP, 44,100 SAMPLES A SECOND
WAV for short effects, Ogg for music. Loop settings are not the same in both.
all_texts: WAV for short effects; Ogg Vorbis for music, speech and long sounds.
4 S MUSIC LOOP, 44,100 SAMPLES A SECOND
WAV for short effects, Ogg for music. Loop settings are not the same in both.

new_texts: Where a looping sound jumps back to; WAV has begin and end, Ogg only a start offset.
WAV: LOOP MODE FORWARD, BEGIN 0, END 176,399
Ogg has only the start offset: cut the file at a bar line first.
At the loop end, playback jumps back to the begin. The ends must match.
all_texts: WAV for short effects; Ogg Vorbis for music, speech and long sounds.

slides.title: AudioStreamPlayer and polyphony

new_texts: Godot node that plays sound with no position.
AudioStreamPlayer2D: pans and fades with position
AudioStreamPlayer3D: the same, in a 3D world
A player node plays a stream and sends it to a bus. The plain one has no position.

new_texts: How many copies of a sound can play at once; Godot's default is 1.
MAX_POLYPHONY = 1 (DEFAULT): EACH PLAY CUTS THE LAST
three play() calls, 40 ms apart, on a 60 ms click
Default is one voice: a second play() cuts the first, so fast hits stutter.

slides.title: Buses, decibels, headroom and clipping
slides.source: Source: Chapter 12, “Buses: where levels live”; glossary, 2D art and sound assets.
slides.notes: Music at −12 dB is from Chapter 12. Amplitudes and percentages are computed.
slides.picture: Players routed to Music and SFX buses and then Master. Then decibel values and their amplitudes. Then a sine below the maximum with headroom. Then the same sine turned up until its peaks flatten.

new_texts: A channel that sounds are routed through for shared volume and effects.
each bus can be lowered, ducked or muted on its own
A bus is a shared mixing point: levels live there, not in the file.
all_texts: A channel that sounds are routed through for shared volume and effects.
each bus can be lowered, ducked or muted on its own
A bus is a shared mixing point: levels live there, not in the file.

new_texts: every −6 dB about halves the amplitude
Decibels are logarithmic. Halving the amplitude is −6 dB, so the scale stays short.
all_texts: A channel that sounds are routed through for shared volume and effects.
every −6 dB about halves the amplitude
Decibels are logarithmic. Halving the amplitude is −6 dB, so the scale stays short.

new_texts: Spare level left below the maximum.
Peak 0.5 leaves 6.02 dB of headroom. That space is for loud moments.
all_texts: A channel that sounds are routed through for shared volume and effects.
Spare level left below the maximum.

new_texts: Distortion when a signal exceeds the maximum level.
THE SAME SINE, TURNED UP BY 7.60 DB
gain 7.60 dB over the first sine; the tops are cut
Past the maximum the tops flatten. That is distortion you hear as a crackle.
